execution_context.file_location: malicious document or executable delivered via phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Code that exfiltrates files to Dropbox and receives commands from Dropbox (as described in the Turla backdoor).
malicious_snippets.code_language: unknown (likely C/C++ or Python, as typical for Turla tools)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code scans the filesystem for documents, uploads them to a Dropbox account via the Dropbox API, and polls Dropbox for new command files, enabling remote control and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of a legitimate cloud storage service (Dropbox) for command-and-control and data exfiltration is a hallmark of advanced persistent threats and is rarely seen in legitimate software.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not exfiltrate user documents to third-party cloud accounts or use cloud storage as a command channel.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate backup tools may upload files to Dropbox, but only with user consent and clear configuration.
key_indicators: Network connections to Dropbox API from unexpected processes

execution_context.file_location: malicious executable or script delivered via phishing or lateral movement

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Trickbot module targeting UEFI vulnerabilities to install a bootkit for persistence.
malicious_snippets.code_language: likely C/C++ (as typical for Trickbot modules)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code exploits UEFI vulnerabilities to write a bootkit to the system firmware, ensuring malware persists even after OS reinstallation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Modifying UEFI firmware is highly privileged and almost never performed by legitimate userland applications.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not write to UEFI or install bootkits.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Firmware update utilities may write to UEFI, but only with explicit user action and vendor signatures.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Crypto mining malware distributed by BISMUTH group, running mining operations on infected hosts.
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (often C/C++, Go, or compiled binaries)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code hijacks system CPU/GPU resources to mine cryptocurrency, sending mining results to attacker-controlled wallets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized crypto mining consumes system resources and is a common monetization tactic for malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not mine cryptocurrency without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: User-installed mining software with explicit consent.
key_indicators: High CPU/GPU usage by unknown processes

attack_chain.action: Victim receives phishing email with malicious attachment or link (Turla, Trickbot, BISMUTH).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code execution on victim system

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes, establishing persistence and/or exfiltrating data (Turla backdoor, Trickbot UEFI bootkit, BISMUTH miner).
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration, system compromise, or resource hijacking

attack_chain.action: Exfiltration of sensitive documents (Turla), persistent compromise (Trickbot), or ongoing crypto mining (BISMUTH).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves objectives: espionage, persistence, or monetization

behavioral_signatures: Unauthorized access to user documents and upload to cloud storage (Dropbox, etc.)
Network connections to cloud storage APIs from non-standard processes
Modification of UEFI firmware or boot process
Unusual, sustained high CPU/GPU usage by unknown processes
Outbound connections to cryptocurrency mining pools
file_indicators: Unknown executables or scripts in user download or temp directories
Persistence mechanisms in firmware or bootloader
Unexpected scheduled tasks or autorun entries
network_indicators: Connections to api.dropbox.com or other cloud storage APIs from non-browser processes
Connections to known mining pool domains/IPs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized access to user documents and uploads to cloud storage services, especially from processes not associated with legitimate backup tools. Detect attempts to access or modify UEFI firmware regions. Monitor for high CPU/GPU usage by unknown processes and outbound connections to mining pools. Correlate phishing email delivery with subsequent suspicious process execution.
